summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has been formalised as state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records that policy operating in the city directly, including intensified practices of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ residents that obstruct access to housing.

The same monitoring counts six violations of the right to life across Turkey in 2025, three recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the group most affected. Torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled, rising to 89 from 51. One LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on civil-society monitoring rather than government record-keeping.

Identity checks are deployed against trans women as a profiling exercise. On 31 July 2025 police stopped around 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district for ID checks, recorded their names and took video of them; the reporting on the roundup characterised the operation plainly as profiling. Any foreign visitor stopped in comparable circumstances presents documents for inspection, and a gender marker that does not match presentation is exposed at that moment.

Public assembly for Pride has been prohibited in İstanbul for a decade. The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned pride parades since 2015 on security and public-order grounds, using water cannon on 29 June 2015. The 2014 march had drawn over 100,000 participants, the largest LGBT event in Turkey's history. Suppression escalated in the years that followed: blockades and tear gas in 2021 with 25 people arrested; 373 arrested in 2022 as public transport to Taksim Square was shut down; 113 arrests in 2023; and 11 arrests in 2024, three of them minors, after organisers moved İstanbul Pride to non-Taksim public spaces and issued fake meeting calls to thwart police.

The June 2022 operation shows the scale of the response a Pride gathering can draw. On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the nearby Cihangir neighbourhood, shut down public transport to the square and detained 373 people, among them AFP photojournalist Bülent Kılıç, who were released after a night in custody according to Kaos GL. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all Pride Week events for seven days, and eight more people were detained at a Pride march in İzmir. Duvar English reported on 27 June 2022 that Turkish authorities have banned Pride since 2014 and that police crackdowns on the parades have grown harsher over the years.
tangentialFactors:
Arrest totals at İstanbul Pride rose and then fell: 25 in 2021, 373 in 2022, 113 in 2023 and 11 in 2024. Organisers adapted to the lower but still present risk by relocating the march to public spaces away from Taksim and issuing decoy meeting calls, which suggests the operational ban is enforced against gatherings wherever they assemble rather than against a single fixed route.

Bans have been issued at district level and across whole programmes. The Kadıköy and Beyoğlu district governor's offices prohibited all Pride Week events for seven days in 2022, a wider measure than refusal of a single parade permit.

Foreign nationals present at these demonstrations have been detained alongside Turkish participants. The 2022 detentions included a photojournalist working for a foreign news agency, released after a night in custody.

The same suppression pattern appears outside İstanbul: eight further detentions at a Pride march in İzmir during the same 2022 period, indicating a nationwide rather than purely municipal practice.

Because the state records no official hate-crime statistics, evidence about violence and about detention totals is assembled entirely by civil-society monitors such as Kaos GL, which constrains what can be verified against official data.

outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: sources disagree on when the İstanbul governorship's parade bans began. One account states bans have been in place since 2015 with water cannon used on 29 June 2015; another reports that Turkish authorities have banned Pride since 2014. Both dates are carried here without reconciliation.

Unresolved: the inventory provides no count for the sealed or closed homes referenced in the 2025 report, so the scale of that practice in İstanbul cannot be stated.

Unresolved: the sources record release of the 373 people detained in 2022 after a night in custody but do not state whether charges were subsequently brought against any of them, or against those detained in 2021, 2023 or 2024.

Not sourced here: the legal basis invoked for the 31 July 2025 ID checks, and whether those checks were accompanied by any citation of offence. The reporting characterises the operation as profiling; it does not set out the statutory power relied on.

Not sourced here: whether a Pride ban has been issued for 2026. The most recent documented refusal covers the periods reported through 2025.
